title: Thermal heat-current cumulant ratios can be arbitrarily negative: three-state counterexamples to two sign conjectures
shortTitle: Negative heat cumulants without quantum effects
oneLine: Two conjectured sign rules for heat-current fluctuations in classical thermal networks are false: three states with a rarely visited trap make the third and fourth cumulant ratios arbitrarily negative at fixed thermodynamic data, while variance-based bounds remain intact.
abstract: Ptaszyński (Physical Review E 106, 024119, 2022) conjectured, from random-network calculations, that the heat-current cumulant ratios C3/C1 and C4/C2 are nonnegative in classical Markov systems driven only by temperature differences, so that a negative value could certify non-thermal or non-classical driving. This candidate gives exact three-state counterexamples that obey bathwise local detailed balance with two baths. After a common rescaling of all rates, which leaves both ratios unchanged, a fully connected family keeps the energies, temperatures, stationary probabilities, mean heat current and entropy production fixed while both ratios tend to minus infinity like ε^-2. In the standard state-jump model with one counted bath, two states can never violate either sign. The mechanism is classical slow switching through a weakly coupled trap state, and the divergence tracks the variance: the variance-normalised ratios tend to -9/4 and -3/4 in that family, and the thermodynamic uncertainty relation is untouched. For positive mean and variance a kinetic lower bound in terms of the spectral separation of the stationary eigenvalue captures the ε^-2 rate. With six states even the normalised ratios are unbounded below. Violations need rate separations of order 10^2, which is why random sampling rarely finds them. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

keyResults: Counterexample in the conjectured class (Section 3, exact certificate): a three-state, two-bath network obeying local detailed balance has C3/C1 ≈ −6415 and C4/C2 ≈ −54732 at ε = 10⁻³; K < 0 for ε < 0.0667 and S < 0 for ε < 0.0069.

Weak-trap mechanism (Theorem 4.3, proof): a trap reached through a weak edge gives C3/C1 and C4/C2 ∝ −ε⁻² exactly when (3 − √5)/2 < U/V < 1; every thermal two-state conductor with a trap at the energy of its lower state, joined by an unobserved-bath edge with equal in and out prefactors, lands in this region (Corollary 4.4).

Fixed thermodynamic data (Theorem 5.1, proof and exact certificate): with distinct energies (0, 2, 1), all twelve bath-resolved rates positive, stationary law (40, 5, 18)/63, C1 = 40/63 and fixed entropy production, S = −16/(21609 ε²) + O(ε⁻¹) and K = −16/(64827 ε²) + O(ε⁻¹). No lower bound depending only on these data exists.

What survives (Section 6, proofs): the divergence tracks the variance; the normalised ratios C3C1/C2² and C4C1²/C2³ tend to −9/4 and −3/4 in that family, and in the trap family the normalised kurtosis limit is at least −15/4 (attained). The thermodynamic uncertainty relation holds throughout. With six states both normalised ratios are unbounded below.

Kinetic bound (Theorem 6.3, proof): |Cn| ≤ n!(g/2)(E_max/ℓ)ⁿ in terms of the spectral separation g; if C1 > 0 (resp. C2 > 0) this bounds S (resp. K) below with the correct ε⁻² rate, so very negative ratios require slow kinetics.
Minimality (Proposition 7.1, proof): in the standard state-jump model with one counted bath, two states give C2 > 0, C4 > 0 and C3/C1 ≥ E²/4.

narration: Negative heat fluctuations need no quantum explanation. An Evidence Press briefing. When a tiny device sits between a hot and a cold reservoir, heat flows through it in random bursts. The average flow is the first statistic people measure. The third and fourth statistics, called cumulants, describe whether the flow is lopsided and how heavy its tails are. In 2022, the physicist Ptaszyński found that in more than thirty thousand random classical models driven only by temperature differences, two ratios of these statistics were never negative. He conjectured that they never are. If true, a negative ratio would be a cheap test for quantum effects or for some driving other than heat. Using models with just three states, this release shows that the conjecture is false. Picture a conductor that occasionally falls into an idle trap state, which it enters rarely and leaves slowly. Its heat flow switches between running and pausing, like a telegraph signal. Rare long pauses make both ratios negative, and they can be made as negative as you like while the energies, temperatures and average heat flow stay fixed. Two states can never do this in the standard model. What still holds: bounds based on the variance, such as the thermodynamic uncertainty relation, are untouched. The paper also proves a kinetic bound: very negative ratios require slow relaxation, which can be checked directly. So a negative ratio does not, by itself, certify quantum or non-thermal driving; slow switching must be ruled out first. The results have written proofs and exact computer checks. This is an anonymous, AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate, not peer reviewed or independently reproduced. Published on 27 October 2026, its paper and evidence are linked from the Evidence Press release page. This briefing uses an AI-generated voice and is not additional scientific evidence.

decisionObject.description: Exact three-state, two-bath thermal networks with local detailed balance refute Ptaszyński's (2022) conjectures C3/C1 ≥ 0 and C4/C2 ≥ 0 for heat currents; a full-support family drives both ratios to −∞ at fixed energies, temperatures, stationary law, mean heat current and entropy production.
decisionObject.scope: Finite classical continuous-time Markov jump processes with bathwise local detailed balance and heat counted into one bath by state-energy jumps, as in Ptaszyński (2022), Section III. Long-time cumulants only; the source's other inequalities and quantum models are not addressed.
